title: Job's ending (Job 42)
hookLine: Job prays for his friends, and his daughters are named and given an inheritance

cards: Three girls' names from the very last page of the book of Job. It's an odd place for names to come from: a book of loss, accusation and storm. But the ending of Job has surprises in it, and the daughters are one of them.
First, though, the story has unfinished business. Job has seen God. The friends who explained his pain are still standing there.
And God has something to say to them.

teach.b: First, Job answers the whirlwind. In the King James Bible: "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee." He doesn't get an explanation.
He gets an encounter, and it's enough to quiet him.

Then the book switches back to prose, and God turns to Eliphaz: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath."

Job, who cursed his birthday and argued with God for chapters, spoke rightly. The friends, who defended God with tidy rules, did not. Honest complaint, the book suggests, is closer to the truth than a neat explanation.
Then the turn. The friends must bring an offering, and Job must pray for them, the men who hurt him.

teach.h: WHEN HE PRAYED FOR HIS FRIENDS
teach.b: "And the LORD turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before." That's where the healing turns. Then the family.

Job has seven sons and three daughters again. The sons aren't named. The daughters are: Jemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch, names some readers take to mean dove, cassia, a fragrant spice, and a horn of eye paint.
And their father "gave them inheritance among their brethren." In the law in Numbers, daughters inherit when there are no sons; here they inherit alongside their brothers.
Some readers are uneasy that new children are counted as restoration, and the book doesn't say the grief was erased.
It ends simply: Job died, "being old and full of days."

how: Following Jesus's command to pray for those who wrong them, many Christians include people who have hurt them in their daily prayers, and Job's prayer for his friends is often cited as an example.

o: Job finally learns why he suffered, and forgives his God
Job's friends apologize, and his first children come back

games.q: what happens at the end — tap the pairs.
p: told he had not spoken rightly

s: at the end, God says the friends spoke rightly
God says Job spoke rightly, and the friends did not.
Job's fortunes turn when he prays for his friends
"the LORD turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends."
the book names Job's new sons and daughters
only the daughters are named: Jemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch.

games.q: God has told your friends they were wrong about you. they must bring an offering, and you are asked to pray for them. what do you do?
o: pray, but only after they apologize.
games.why: Job prays for them, and the book says that's when "the LORD turned the captivity of Job."

practice: This one is hard, so go gently: bring to mind someone who hurt you, and if the deepest wound is too much today, choose a smaller one, a sharp word, a careless friend. You don't have to excuse what they did; Job didn't.
If you pray, ask God's good for them, simply, even through clenched teeth; if not, try wishing them well for one breath, then another.

wordCard.voice: Job's ending. Job sees God, prays for the friends who hurt him, and gives his named daughters an inheritance.

orig.note: Hebrew: Jemima, Job's first daughter. the name is often taken to mean dove.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for the friends. Even the ones who got it wrong. Day four hundred forty-nine, done.
